KernelGenBench: A Multi-Source and Multi-Chip Benchmark for LLM-based Kernel Generation

Peiyu Zang Affiliation: Beijing Normal University Affiliation: BAAI Email: 202421130105@mail.bnu.edu.cn    Jian Tao Affiliation: BAAI Email: liuguang@baai.ac.cn    Jialing Zhang Affiliation: Beijing Jiaotong University Affiliation: BAAI    Yichen Yuan Affiliation: Institute of Automation, CAS Affiliation: BAAI    Wentao Zhang Affiliation: Peking University    Guang Liu ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: BAAI    Yonghua Lin Affiliation: BAAI
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) have significantly increased the demand for efficient accelerator kernels, but kernel development remains a highly specialized and labor-intensive task. The recent rise of LLMs and agentic frameworks offers a promising pathway toward automatic kernel generation. However, despite rapid progress, there is still no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms. We present KernelGenBench11 1 Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/flagos-ai/KernelGenBench., a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. It comprises two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source), evaluating 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip), measuring performance portability across five alternative hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. Our large-scale evaluation, consuming over 15 billion tokens, shows: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling methods, while cuBLAS operators are the most challenging across all methods; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with even state-of-the-art kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation remains highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaches 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling approaches.

1 Introduction

The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has significantly increased the demand for efficient accelerator kernels that are critical for high-performance model execution. However, designing such kernels remains a challenging task that requires deep expertise in low-level programming, hardware architectures, and performance optimization. Recently, the emergence of LLMs and agentic frameworks has created new opportunities for automatically generating GPU kernels. Existing work has primarily focused on NVIDIA-centric CUDA and Triton kernels [1], which continue to dominate current research and deployment settings. These advances raise the possibility of democratizing a process that has traditionally required significant domain expertise.

However, despite rapid progress in LLM-based kernel generation, there is still no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate their effectiveness and real-world utility. Existing high-level code generation benchmarks [2, 3] focus primarily on functional correctness, while low-level kernels additionally require hardware efficiency [4, 5]. Meanwhile, existing kernel benchmarks [6, 7] remain narrowly scoped, typically focusing on single-source operators within restricted ecosystems, and fail to capture the complexity of real-world deployment scenarios across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms.

To address this gap, we introduce KernelGenBench, a multi-source and multi-chip benchmark that systematically evaluates LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms, ensuring cross-platform portability beyond traditional CUDA lock-in [8, 9, 10]. KernelGenBench consists of two complementary sub-benchmarks:

  • •

    KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source): Evaluates kernel generation across 210 operators spanning PyTorch ATen [11], vLLM [12], and cuBLAS baselines.

  • •

    KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip): Assesses performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator ATen subset.

To enable robust and realistic evaluation, we design a production-aligned execution framework with a distributed sandbox infrastructure and a three-tier anti-hack mechanism that prevents benchmark evasion. We also introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol that jointly measures functional correctness, execution speedup, and agentic cost efficiency.

We conducted extensive experiments consuming over 15 billion tokens. Our experiments show several key findings. (1) Agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling approaches, but operator source imposes a clear difficulty hierarchy: ATen operators are the most tractable, vLLM operators are the hardest to generate correctly but offer the greatest speedup potential, and cuBLAS operators remain the most challenging overall due to severe optimization ceilings across all methods. (2) Generation performance varies substantially across hardware platforms, exposing major portability challenges, with even state-of-the-art kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E). (3) Although autonomous agentic frameworks improve correctness through iterative debugging and optimization, they remain highly cost-intensive, with specialized methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaches 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling approaches.

2 Related Work

2.1 LLM-Driven Kernel Generation

Recent work on automated accelerator kernel generation spans two tracks [13]. On the model side, approaches include supervised fine-tuning on compiler-generated datasets [14], reinforcement learning with compilation feedback [15], and execution-grounded post-training on industrial workloads [16]. However, static inference restricts optimization to a single pass, motivating iterative agentic systems that autonomously debug and optimize Triton code via execution-driven reinforcement [17], evolutionary search [18], and runtime log exploitation [19]. While these systems have proven effective at achieving functional correctness, their rapid advancement shifts the bottleneck to the urgent need for rigorous, large-scale evaluation benchmarks.

2.2 Limitations of Existing Benchmarks

As kernel agents rapidly mature, existing benchmarks struggle to adequately evaluate their boundaries, particularly in cross-platform scenarios and multi-source operator generation. We categorize current evaluation limitations along these two dimensions:

Single-source constraints. KernelBench [6] and TritonBench [7] pioneered execution-based evaluation, but their exclusive focus on standardized PyTorch primitives has allowed kernel-specialized agents to reach near 100% correctness, creating an illusion of solvedness [20]. BackendBench [21] integrates Triton into PyTorch but still operates at a high abstraction level, lacking the unstructured engineering complexity of production-grade libraries like vLLM or cuBLAS. Furthermore, inspired by SWE-bench [22] in general software engineering, we argue that kernel evaluation must move beyond single-pass correctness to assess closed-loop agentic debugging and its associated token costs.

Single-hardware lock-in. The vast majority of kernel benchmarks remain strictly confined to the NVIDIA ecosystem. FlashInfer-Bench [23] and SOL-ExecBench [24] introduce valuable performance metrics but target only single-GPU NVIDIA settings. While MultiKernelBench [25] makes a preliminary attempt at cross-platform evaluation, it lacks a unified verification pipeline and consistent execution baselines. Consequently, no existing benchmark has systematically measured the severe performance portability gap—the divergence in execution speedup caused by fragmented compiler maturities across heterogeneous hardware platforms.

3 KernelGenBench

We introduce KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark comprising two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS and KernelGenBench-MC, as illustrated in Figure 1.

3.1 KernelGenBench-MS

To measure the true boundaries of kernel generation capabilities, KernelGenBench-MS is anchored on a stable NVIDIA hardware baseline (controlling for compiler maturity) and curates 210 operators from three complementary sources, each representing a distinct category of real-world kernel workloads: framework-level open-source operators (PyTorch ATen), CUDA open-source library operators (vLLM), and CUDA closed-source library operators (cuBLAS). A key design principle is that we explicitly provide detailed API signatures for all operators, and the generated Triton kernels must exactly match these specifications, enabling them to serve as drop-in replacements for production [26]. All prompt contexts are constructed by HPC engineers following actual development workflows (Appendix A). Full operator lists are in Appendix B.

Source 1: PyTorch ATen Operators (110 problems). We systematically filter out of the 900+ torch.ops.aten APIs: the top-50 most frequent operators are extracted from real training traces of 2,907 open-source models, and 60 long-tail operators are uniformly sampled. Each operator API is an independent problem (e.g., torch.abs and torch.abs_ are two separate problems), requiring the model to implement all overload variants. Prompts are constructed by dynamically extracting the FunctionSchema and official docstrings. The baseline directly invokes native ATen APIs.

Source 2: vLLM Operators (50 problems). We select operators with standalone CUDA implementations from vLLM, covering attention mechanisms (e.g., paged_attention_v1), KV cache management and mixed-precision quantization (FP8/AWQ).22 2 All vLLM evaluations use v0.13.0 in this paper. This subset tests whether models can generate the acceleration kernels used in real-world LLM inference.

Source 3: cuBLAS Operators (50 problems). We designate the cuBLAS closed-source dynamic library as the absolute performance baseline.33 3 All cuBLAS evaluations use v12.4 in this paper. Critically, the baseline loads libcublas.so directly via ctypes.cdll, bypassing all high-level wrappers. To construct a balanced problem set, we first identify the 10 most frequently invoked cuBLAS routines via profiling traces and expand them across precision and batching modes. Furthermore, to prevent the evaluation from over-indexing on a single operator family (e.g., where mastering one GEMM variant allows trivial generalization to all others), we strategically sample standard versions of other functionally diverse BLAS routines. This compels the model to match proprietary performance across a broad spectrum of linear algebra tasks without relying on external libraries. Table 1 illustrates the fine-grained API fragmentation using GEMM as an example.

3.2 KernelGenBench-MC

To systematically evaluate models’ kernel generation capabilities across heterogeneous hardware platforms, KernelGenBench-MC establishes a unified evaluation framework. To control for task complexity, this sub-benchmark relies exclusively on the ATen operator subset.

The framework natively targets six distinct architectures: NVIDIA A100 and five alternative hardware platforms (Platform A–E), whose identities are anonymized at their request due to confidentiality agreements. These platforms represent diverse architectural paradigms and ecosystem maturity levels: CUDA-compatible architectures with established toolchains, proprietary instruction sets with vendor-specific software stacks, and emerging accelerators with nascent compiler infrastructures. Rather than testing in isolation, KernelGenBench-MC provides a single execution pipeline where hardware is automatically detected. It injects hardware-specific prompt templates and applies adaptive numerical tolerances and anti-hack configurations per platform (details in Appendix C), creating the first standardized arena for heterogeneous Triton evaluation.

3.3 Evaluation Framework

Both sub-benchmarks are powered by a shared evaluation infrastructure that executes the following workflow. The distributed sandbox infrastructure is detailed in Appendix D.

Kernel Generation. We evaluate methods across two paradigms: (1) LLM Sampling Methods—direct zero-shot and multi-sample generation (Pass@1, Pass@5) [27] without execution feedback (pseudocode in Appendix E), evaluating Opus-4.6, GLM-5.0, Qwen3.5-27B, and MiniMax M-2.5; (2) Agent-Based Methods—autonomous coding agents with execution feedback loops, including vanilla agentic frameworks (Claude Code, OpenCode) and kernel-specialized agents (AutoKernel [28], AKO4all [29], CUDA Optimized Skill [30]).

Verification. Generated kernels serve as input to the unified verify engine. Unlike prior benchmarks that evaluate fixed single-shape inputs [6], we construct a combinatorial test suite of kik_{i} distinct test cases per operator by taking the Cartesian product of core semantic parameters (e.g., dim, transpose) alongside shape, data type, and memory layout (details in Appendix F). Kernels are mounted directly into PyTorch’s dispatch tree via torch.library, ensuring drop-in replaceability. A kernel is considered correct only when it passes numerical validation across all kik_{i} test cases.

Anti-Hack Architecture. To guard against benchmark hacking [31] (e.g., bypassing Triton compilation by calling pre-compiled backend APIs), we deploy a three-tier interception mechanism:

  • •

    L1: AST Static Scan: Parses the generated abstract syntax tree to block blacklisted calls (e.g., torch.ops.aten.*, import vllm, and ctypes) and dynamic injection bypasses.

  • •

    L2: Ghost Replay: First executes the kernel normally to capture outputs, then replaces the @triton.jit-decorated function with a no-op in memory and replays; identical outputs logically prove the Triton kernel was never invoked, triggering a cheating flag.

  • •

    L3: Hardware Profiling: Uses torch.profiler to ensure Triton-specific signatures exist in low-level trace logs. This layer operates exclusively on NVIDIA hardware; heterogeneous platforms rely on the first two layers due to the absence of equivalent profiling tools.

Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate correctness, performance, and cost efficiency. Clean pass rate counts an operator as successful only when all kik_{i} test cases pass both numerical validation and the three-layer anti-hack check. For performance, we compute a two-level geometric mean [32, 33]: first across the kik_{i} test cases to obtain operator-level speedup SiS_{i}, then across all operators to obtain the global speedup. Speedup distribution metrics (fastp) are detailed in Appendix G. For agentic methods, we track total tokens, tokens per success (total tokens divided by passed operators), and total wall time (cumulative per-operator solving duration, parallelism-agnostic).

4 Experiments and Evaluation

In this section, we deploy KernelGenBench to evaluate LLMs and agentic frameworks across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms.

4.1 Experimental Setup

We deploy the evaluation suite across six dedicated full-node hardware platforms: NVIDIA A100 and five alternative hardware platforms (Platform A–E). The full 210-operator problem set is evaluated on the NVIDIA baseline, while the 110-operator ATen subset is used to benchmark cross-platform portability. For all language models, we use temperature=0 for Pass@1 generation and temperature=0.8 for Pass@5, with a context window limit of max_tokens=16384 and a unified 30-minute wall-clock timeout per operator task. Evaluated paradigms are detailed in Section 3.3. Results for legacy models are deferred to Appendix H. All agent results are single-trajectory measurements due to cost constraints; we therefore interpret cross-method differences below 5 pp cautiously.

4.2 KernelGenBench-MS: Multi-Source Evaluation

We evaluate all methods on NVIDIA A100 across the full 210-operator suite. Table 2 presents the comprehensive results.

Finding 1: Model and Method Capabilities. Claude Code (Opus-4.6) achieves the highest overall accuracy at 87%, while AutoKernel (Qwen3.5-27b) achieves the highest overall speedup at 1.02×\times. Comparing the two top performers shows a fundamental trade-off: Claude Code outperforms the kernel-specialized AKO4all (Opus-4.6) at 83% accuracy by 4 pp, but AKO4all achieves 0.97×\times speedup versus Claude Code’s 0.78×\times. Kernel-specialized agents prioritize performance optimization over correctness, sacrificing functional correctness on edge cases to maximize speedup. By contrast, vanilla agentic frameworks allocate more iterations to debugging and correctness verification, producing higher pass rates at the cost of performance. Speedup distribution metrics (fastp) for all configurations are detailed in Appendix I.

Breaking down by operator source shows where specialization pays off. On ATen operators, both Claude Code and OpenCode with Opus-4.6 reach 92% accuracy, while kernel-specialized agents (AKO4all, AutoKernel with GLM-5.0/Qwen3.5-27b) achieve 1.00×\times speedup, perfectly matching the baseline. On vLLM operators, Claude Code (Opus-4.6) leads in accuracy at 68%, but AutoKernel (Qwen3.5-27b) delivers 1.63×\times speedup—the highest across all sources—demonstrating that specialized agents perform well at performance optimization on complex operators. On cuBLAS operators, Claude Code (Opus-4.6) achieves 94% accuracy, but even the best speedup (AutoKernel Qwen at 0.80×\times) remains below the proprietary baseline. Model-specific generation bottlenecks and anti-hack interception patterns are detailed in Appendix J.

Finding 2: Operator-Source Difficulty Hierarchy. A strict, model-agnostic difficulty hierarchy emerges across the three operator sources. ATen operators are the most tractable: even weaker models achieve reasonable accuracy (e.g., Claude Code with MiniMax reaches 69%), and speedup consistently clusters around 0.8–1.0×\times, matching the framework baseline. This reflects ATen’s design as a high-level framework API with well-defined semantics and moderate performance requirements.

vLLM operators present the opposite profile—functional correctness is extremely challenging (accuracy drops sharply, e.g., Claude Code with MiniMax falls to 26%), but when successfully generated, they deliver genuine acceleration potential (AKO4all achieves 1.62×\times, AutoKernel with Qwen reaches 1.63×\times). This difficulty is due to vLLM’s complex inference-specific operators (paged attention, KV cache management, mixed-precision quantization), which require intricate memory layouts and algorithmic understanding that LLMs struggle to implement correctly. However, the baseline implementations are not heavily hand-tuned, leaving room for optimization when correctness is achieved.

cuBLAS operators occupy the middle ground: moderate accuracy is achievable (Claude Code with Opus reaches 94%), but speedup is universally capped—virtually all configurations cluster tightly around 0.50×\times, unable to exceed the hand-tuned proprietary baseline. This performance ceiling reflects cuBLAS’s status as a closed-source, heavily optimized library representing decades of expert engineering. The baseline directly loads libcublas.so via ctypes, bypassing all high-level wrappers, making it nearly impossible for LLM-generated Triton kernels to match proprietary BLAS performance. This hierarchy shows that ATen serves as the tractable baseline, vLLM tests optimization capability on complex kernels, and cuBLAS exposes the fundamental difficulty of matching closed-source performance.

4.3 KernelGenBench-MC: Cross-Platform Evaluation

We extend the evaluation of the 110 ATen operators across six hardware platforms. Table 3 presents the comprehensive results.

Finding 1: Model and Method Capabilities Across Platforms. For accuracy, Claude Code (Opus-4.6) consistently achieves the highest rates across most platforms: 92% on NVIDIA, 89% on Platform A, 93% on Platform B, 88% on Platform C, and 96% on Platform D; Platform E is the exception, where Claude Code (MiniMax M-2.5) reaches 69%. For speedup, kernel-specialized agents dominate: AKO4all (Opus-4.6) achieves the best overall performance with 1.00×\times on NVIDIA, 1.08×\times on Platform C, 1.12×\times on Platform D, and 1.07×\times on Platform E, while AutoKernel (MiniMax M-2.5) reaches the highest single-platform speedup at 1.36×\times on Platform B. However, kernel-specialized agents exhibit severe accuracy variance across platforms: AKO4all ranges from 89% on NVIDIA to 80% on Platform E, while AutoKernel (Qwen3.5-27b) spans 75% on Platform B down to 21% on Platform E, showing that even state-of-the-art specialized methods struggle with cross-platform portability.

This divergence is due to how methods utilize platform-specific information. Vanilla agentic frameworks like Claude Code provide minimal initial context but include hardware-specific constraints (e.g., API limitations, type strictness) in the prompt; agents actively leverage this information during debugging, adapting their implementations to platform quirks. Kernel-specialized agents, by contrast, focus heavily on performance tuning (profiling, block-size search, memory-access optimization) and often overlook the provided platform constraints, leading to compilation failures or runtime errors on non-NVIDIA backends despite achieving higher speedup when kernels do compile successfully.

Finding 2: Platform-Specific Performance Divergence. Cross-platform evaluation exposes severe performance heterogeneity. Platform A suffers from a catastrophic speedup collapse: Claude Code (Opus-4.6) maintains 89% accuracy but achieves only 0.18×\times speedup, the lowest across all platforms. This 4.8×\times degradation relative to NVIDIA (0.86×\times) exposes unoptimized backend implementations despite functional correctness. Platform E exhibits the opposite failure mode—accuracy collapse: Claude Code with Qwen3.5-27b drops to 23%, and AutoKernel variants fall to 21–25%, significantly lower than other platforms (typically 60–90%). This reflects immature vendor compilers that frequently hang or crash when processing unstructured LLM-generated code, leading to compilation timeouts. Furthermore, non-NVIDIA platforms incur massive compilation overheads: Platform A requires 2.1×\times tokens and 2.0×\times time relative to NVIDIA (Figure 2), forcing agents to burn iteration budgets on compilation debugging rather than kernel optimization.

Finding 3: Cross-Platform Cost Overhead. Non-NVIDIA platforms incur massive compilation overheads, as quantified in Figure 2 (right panel). Platform A exhibits the most severe overhead: 173M total tokens (2.06×\times NVIDIA’s 84M baseline) and 18 hours (2.00×\times NVIDIA’s 9 hours). Platform B requires 128M tokens (1.52×\times) and 16 hours (1.78×\times), while Platforms C, D, and E consume 107–123M tokens (1.27–1.46×\times) and 15–16 hours (1.67–1.78×\times). This overhead is not algorithmic; it is purely ecosystem friction from immature vendor compilers and incomplete Triton backend support.

The root cause is that models lack prior exposure to heterogeneous hardware constraints during pretraining. When generating kernels for alternative platforms, agents must iteratively discover platform-specific limitations through trial and error: API availability (e.g., missing tl.acosh or tl.math.tanh), type system strictness (mixed int32/int64 loops that compile silently on CUDA but raise hard errors elsewhere), pointer addressing modes (32-bit vs 64-bit), and LLVM IR compatibility gaps. Each compilation failure forces the agent to burn tokens diagnosing opaque backend errors, adjusting code to satisfy undocumented constraints, and re-attempting compilation, consuming iteration budgets that would otherwise be spent on functional correctness or performance optimization. Platform A’s 2×\times overhead directly reflects its backend’s fragility: frequent compilation hangs and cryptic error messages force agents into extended debugging cycles, while Platform E’s compiler instability (leading to the 21–25% accuracy collapse noted in Finding 2) similarly inflates token costs as agents repeatedly retry failed compilations before timing out.

4.4 Accuracy-Speedup Gap

Figure 3 plots per-operator accuracy against speedup on the NVIDIA baseline across 16 configurations. A systematic pattern emerges: accuracy spans the full range (2% for MiniMax Pass@1 to 87% for Claude Code Opus-4.6), while speedup clusters tightly in a narrow band (0.62–1.01×\times, with 14 of 16 configurations falling within 0.68–0.83×\times). The two outliers are Qwen3.5 Pass@5 at 1.01×\times (11% accuracy) and MiniMax OpenCode at 0.62×\times (41% accuracy). This divergence indicates survivorship bias: operators that weaker models fail to solve are disproportionately the computationally complex ones, where the baseline is heavily hand-tuned and high speedup is hardest to achieve. Weaker configurations report higher average speedup not because they optimize better, but because they fail the complex tasks and avoid their severe performance penalties (e.g., the 0.50×\times ceiling of cuBLAS). They only survive the simpler operators where matching the baseline (achieving ∼\sim0.8–1.0×\times) is relatively easy. Consequently, speedup comparisons across methods are only meaningful when conditioned on matched operator subsets.

4.5 Trajectory Analysis

Analysis of hundreds of complete LLM and agent trajectories uncovers two distinct failure layers. Universal algorithmic failures occur across all platforms: infinite dispatch recursion (calling the overridden ATen operator internally triggers unbounded recursion), hallucinated Triton APIs (models generate calls to non-existent functions such as tl.pow, tl.einsum, tl.gather), and algorithmically hard operators (matmul, sort, cumsum require cross-block parallel algorithms that agents rarely converge to).

Heterogeneous-platform failures directly explain the accuracy collapse on Platform E: LLVM IR incompatibility triggers PassManager::run failed errors (31 observed occurrences on one platform), 32-bit pointer addressing causes memory errors on large-tensor operators, and missing math APIs (tl.acosh, tl.math.tanh) must be manually reimplemented. Further failure patterns (8 universal and 6 platform-specific) are provided in Appendix K.

4.6 Agentic Cost Efficiency

The introduction of closed-loop execution brings significant economic and time overhead. Table 4 quantifies this cost on the NVIDIA A100 baseline. Kernel-specialized agents universally consume far more tokens and time than vanilla frameworks—their extended iteration budgets are spent optimizing kernel performance. AKO4all is the most extreme case, requiring 904M tokens and 83 hours—over 3×\times the token cost of Claude Code (Opus-4.6) at 263M—achieving 5.19M tokens per successful operator. Across all kernel-specialized methods (AKO4all, CUDA Optimized Skill, AutoKernel variants), the average tokens per successful operator is 5.11M, orders of magnitude higher than vanilla agentic frameworks (1.45–3.30M) and simple LLM sampling approaches. These results highlight the need for more cost-efficient agentic methods that can close the performance gap without prohibitive overhead.

4.7 Ablation: Value of Execution Feedback

To isolate the contribution of execution feedback, we conduct a controlled ablation on Opus-4.6 across the full 210-operator NVIDIA suite. Figure 4 presents the results; the full per-subset breakdown is in Appendix L.

Performance scales tightly with method complexity: Pass@1 (41%) << Pass@5 (57%) << Vanilla Agentic (87%) ≈\approx Kernel-Specialized (83%). Merely placing the model in a naive framework wrapper adds no value: Single-step Agent achieves 44%, nearly identical to Pass@1 at 41%. Autonomous interactive debugging is the true driver of agentic value: Claude Code reaches 87%, a 27 pp jump over standard reflection (Pass@5 Reflection at 60%).

We further identify an exploitation–exploration trap in fixed traceback-based reflection. Even when provided with execution errors, Pass@5 Reflection barely outperforms independent multi-sampling (No-Reflect at 57%) and actually underperforms it on vLLM (24% vs 28%). Code similarity analysis shows that traceback-driven reflection produces 88% average cross-turn similarity (local patching), whereas independent sampling averages 36% (global search). Without the agentic autonomy to write custom test harnesses or dynamically probe intermediate variables, models fed with raw tracebacks over-exploit their first-round implementation and easily get trapped in local optima.

5 Conclusion

We have presented KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark comprising two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (210 operators from three sources) and KernelGenBench-MC (cross-platform verification) for systematically evaluating LLM-driven Triton kernel generation. Our large-scale evaluation shows three findings: agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling approaches, although cuBLAS operators remain the most challenging across all methods; generation accuracy varies dramatically across hardware platforms, with even state-of-the-art kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); and specialized agentic methods incur token costs averaging 5.11 million per successful operator (AKO4all reaches 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling approaches.

Overall, KernelGenBench provides the first comprehensive framework for understanding and advancing LLM-driven kernel generation across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. We open-source the full benchmark suite, evaluation infrastructure, and all agent trajectories to facilitate reproducibility and community extension. Three limitations bound current conclusions. First, the full Multi-Chip ×\times Multi-Source benchmark is absent due to nascent vendor ecosystems, and the current 210-operator suite covers only a fraction of the full ATen and library surface. Second, single-trajectory evaluation is cost-constrained: with over 15 billion tokens consumed, repeated trials are economically prohibitive. Third, the benchmark measures the joint performance of an LLM and its agentic scaffold; systematically decoupling framework heuristics from intrinsic LLM capabilities remains an open challenge. Future work will partner with hardware vendors to complete this unified benchmark, scale toward 900+ ATen operators and additional libraries (cuDNN [34], CUTLASS [35], SGLang [36]), and introduce specialized subsets to assess fine-grained peak performance.

Appendix A Prompt Design

KernelGenBench dynamically constructs structured prompts for each operator rather than relying on vague natural-language descriptions. Table 5 summarizes the prompt template modules and their differences between the LLM Sampling and Agentic evaluation paradigms.

The key difference across the three subsets lies in the “Operator Spec / Baseline Source Injection” module: the ATen subset extracts the full FunctionSchema and all overload variants at runtime; the vLLM subset, lacking public API documentation, directly injects the complete Python source code containing _custom_ops calls; the cuBLAS subset injects a ctypes-based C API call chain (including handle management and pointer mode switching logic).

Figure 5 uses aten::add as an example, showing side-by-side the actual prompts under the LLM Sampling and Agentic paradigms (shared portions abbreviated as [...] for brevity). The prompts shown are for NVIDIA; on alternative platforms, the device-specific references (e.g., “GPU programmer”) are automatically replaced with the corresponding platform-specific terminology, and additional device constraints are appended.

Appendix C Cross-Platform Prompt and Tolerance Configuration

This section details the hardware-specific configurations injected by KernelGenBench-MC for heterogeneous chip evaluation.

Hardware-Aware Prompt Templates. The framework maintains separate prompt template directories per device type (e.g., templates/platform_a/, templates/platform_b/), automatically selecting and assembling the corresponding template at runtime based on detected hardware (e.g., injecting platform-specific import statements and runtime initialization code).

Appendix D Distributed Sandbox Infrastructure

This section details the production-grade dispatch registration and the process isolation and distributed scheduling infrastructure underlying KernelGenBench’s full-node parallel evaluation.

Production-Grade Dispatch Registration. For ATen operators, the system uses register_scanner.py to perform AST scanning and capture @register decorators, force-mounting Triton kernels into PyTorch’s torch.library dispatch tree. All ATen operators are therefore tested under PyTorch’s full low-level dispatch mechanism, not isolated Python function calls.

Full-Node Parallel Evaluation with Process Isolation. To enable full-node utilization, KernelGenBench dispatches all operators in parallel across all available accelerator devices on the machine. Each operator runs in a fully isolated subprocess (multiprocessing spawn), with its own workspace directory and exclusive device assignment—ensuring that a crash, timeout, or device memory corruption in one operator cannot affect any other. The distributed resource scheduler DeviceManager acquires hardware control via kernel-level file locks, recording the holder’s PID and automatically reclaiming locks from crashed processes to prevent permanent device resource leaks. When a subprocess triggers a timeout (300s for correctness, 600s for performance), the parent process sends SIGKILL to destroy the entire process tree.

Adaptive Numerical Tolerance. Numerical comparison of low-level operators is sensitive to floating-point truncation errors. The system implements a dtype- and reduction-dimension-aware adaptive tolerance mechanism: absolute tolerance is computed as atol=10−4×Dreduce\text{atol}=10^{-4}\times D_{\text{reduce}} (DreduceD_{\text{reduce}} is the reduction dimension size), and relative tolerance is calibrated by dtype effective-bit resolution (FP32→10−5,FP16→10−3,BF16→0.016\text{FP32}\to 10^{-5},\text{FP16}\to 10^{-3},\text{BF16}\to 0.016). On NVIDIA GPUs, all three anti-hack layers (L1–L3) are enabled; on heterogeneous platforms, due to torch.profiler adaptation limitations, only L1 static scanning and L2 dual-execution comparison are active.

Appendix E Evaluation Pipeline Algorithm Details

This section provides the full pseudocode for both the agent dispatch pipeline and the LLM Sampling Methods generation pipeline described in Section 3.3.

Formal definition of the LLM Sampling Methods pipeline: For a given operator, the system samples up to kk times sequentially; if the code cic_{i} generated at round ii (i≤ki\leq k) passes correctness verification, the system locks that operator and removes it from the remaining task pool. The Pass@k score for a single operator is thus the indicator 𝕀(∃i≤k,verify(ci)=True)\mathbb{I}(\exists i\leq k,\text{verify}(c_{i})=\text{True}), and the overall clean pass rate is the mean of these indicators across all operators. In multi-round iteration mode, if round tt fails verification, the system extracts the traceback log ete_{t} and constructs the next-round prompt as pt=pt−1⊕ct⊕etp_{t}=p_{t-1}\oplus c_{t}\oplus e_{t}. The framework maintains separate prompt templates for three scenarios—initial generation, performance optimization, and error repair—to avoid information redundancy and semantic conflicts across stages.

Appendix F Stress Test Shape and Dispatch Configurations

This section details the combinatorial test case construction and shape/stride configurations used in KernelGenBench’s parametrized test cases. All constants are defined in accuracy_utils.py.

Extreme Tensor Distributions and Boundary Stress Testing. Test cases deliberately inject many non-aligned long-tail sizes (e.g., 4099940999, odd boundaries constructed as 2d+172^{d}+17), mixed with full-dimensional coverage from scalar () to 5D tensors (16, 7, 57, 32, 29). Minimal-size tests (e.g., shape=(1, 2)) expose kernel launch overhead degradation.

Example: softmax Test Case Construction. For softmax, the semantic parameter is dim (reduction axis). The ki=18k_{i}=18 test cases are the Cartesian product of three axes: shape ∈\in {(1, 256), (4096, 256), (200, 2560, 3)}, dtype ∈\in {float16, float32, bfloat16}, and dim ∈\in {0, 1}. A kernel is counted as passing only if all 18 cases satisfy the adaptive numerical tolerance. The shape and stride grids used across all operator categories are listed in Tables 9 and 10.

Appendix G Speedup Statistical Metrics

The analysis pipeline provides three built-in statistical metrics. Given MM operators that pass correctness verification in an experiment, where the ii-th operator has kik_{i} test cases, the operator-level speedup is defined as:

Si=(∏j=1kiTbase(i,j)Ttriton(i,j))1/kiS_{i}=\left(\prod_{j=1}^{k_{i}}\frac{T_{\text{base}}^{(i,j)}}{T_{\text{triton}}^{(i,j)}}\right)^{1/k_{i}} (1)

The overall speedup is aggregated via a two-level geometric mean:

Soverall=(∏i=1MSi)1/MS_{\text{overall}}=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{M}S_{i}\right)^{1/M} (2)

In addition to GeoMean, the framework includes two robust auxiliary metrics:

1. Median

Sort S1,…,SMS_{1},\ldots,S_{M} and take the middle value:

Median={S(M+1)/2M​ is odd12​(SM/2+SM/2+1)M​ is even\text{Median}=\begin{cases}S_{(M+1)/2}&M\text{ is odd}\\ \frac{1}{2}\left(S_{M/2}+S_{M/2+1}\right)&M\text{ is even}\end{cases}

The median is immune to extreme outliers and provides a robust central tendency estimate when inter-operator speedup variance is large.

2. Interquartile Mean (IQM)

Discard the lowest 25% and highest 25% of sorted operators, then take the arithmetic mean of the middle 50%:

IQM=1|Q3−Q1|​∑i=Q1Q3S(i)\text{IQM}=\frac{1}{|Q_{3}-Q_{1}|}\sum_{i=Q_{1}}^{Q_{3}}S_{(i)}

where Q1=⌊M/4⌋Q_{1}=\lfloor M/4\rfloor, Q3=⌊3​M/4⌋Q_{3}=\lfloor 3M/4\rfloor. IQM balances the statistical efficiency of the mean with the robustness of the median, and has been widely adopted in reinforcement learning benchmarks such as Atari 100k [37, 38], particularly for scenarios with limited samples and skewed distributions.

The three metrics serve different purposes: GeoMean is optimal for multiplicative noise and consistent with system evaluation standards such as SPEC CPU; Median provides the most conservative central estimate; IQM yields a more stable mean after trimming tail noise. All main tables in this paper report GeoMean.

Appendix J Additional Analysis on Generation Behaviors

This section provides supplementary observations regarding model-specific generation bottlenecks and anti-hack interception statistics.

Generation truncation in GLM-5.0. Examining GLM-5.0’s generation logs under Pass@5, we find that a non-trivial fraction of generated kernels are incomplete: the model frequently produces excessive intermediate variables and verbose comments, causing core code logic to be truncated before completion within the uniform 16K max token limit. This generation inefficiency—low effective information per token—directly reduces the number of functionally correct submissions and explains the limited Pass@5 gain observed for GLM-5.0.

Anti-hack interception patterns. Table 16 shows a snapshot of the per-model anti-hack interception counts under Pass@1 and Pass@5. Hacks are heavily concentrated in ATen (29/30 interceptions under Pass@5), with vLLM accounting for almost zero. This is consistent with our findings in Section 4.2: vLLM’s non-standard API forces models to actually write complex logic, making simple shortcut strategies (like calling an existing high-level library function) unviable.

Appendix K Platform-Specific Failure Patterns

Universal Algorithmic Failures. The following bug patterns appear consistently across all platforms and models: (1) Infinite dispatch recursion: calling the overridden ATen operator internally triggers unbounded recursion—the most frequent single failure mode; (2) Hallucinated Triton APIs: models generate calls to non-existent functions such as tl.pow, tl.einsum, and tl.gather; (3) Missing overload variants: bare-name, _out, and _dimname variants required by the dispatch table are frequently omitted; (4) Algorithmically hard operators: matmul, linear, sort, and cumsum require cross-block parallel algorithms (matrix tiling, prefix scan, sorting networks) that agents rarely converge to within the iteration budget; matmul and linear additionally have 10+ overload variants with complex dispatch logic; (5) BLOCK_SIZE conflicts: @triton.autotune decorator definitions clash with manual BLOCK_SIZE assignments in the same kernel; (6) Unsupported Python syntax: Triton rejects break statements and chained boolean expressions that are valid Python; (7) Non-contiguous memory: operators like as_strided and copy_ require non-contiguous memory semantics that Triton’s blocked access model cannot express; (8) Stochastic API divergence: bernoulli and poisson exhibit behavioral differences between Triton’s random API and PyTorch’s reference implementation.

Heterogeneous-Platform Failures. Alternative platforms exhibit additional failure modes beyond the type-system and IR compatibility issues noted in Section 4.5: (1) Pointer/block type mismatch: tl.store(scalar_ptr, block_value) is accepted by CUDA but rejected on certain alternative backends, which require pointer and value types to match; (2) LLVM IR incompatibility: certain Triton IR patterns trigger PassManager::run failed errors on some backends, affecting operators such as fmax, scatter, and full (31 observed occurrences on one platform); (3) 32-bit pointer addressing: some platforms use 32-bit pointer arithmetic versus NVIDIA’s 64-bit, causing memory size too large to fit in 32 bit errors on large-tensor operators like arange and argmax; (4) Missing math APIs: tl.acosh, tl.asin, tl.math.tanh, tl.language.math.pow, and tl.language.math.isinf are absent on certain platforms and must be manually reimplemented using primitive operations; (5) Incomplete BFloat16 support: platforms with partial BFloat16 coverage silently fail on kernels that assume native BFloat16 computation without explicit type fallback; (6) Runtime API failures: certain backends raise runtime errors on memory-sensitive operators (arange, copy_, index_put_, gather) when stride layouts or data-type combinations fall outside supported configurations.
